title: Channel and Parallel.ForEachAsync
sub: Pipelines, completing a channel and limiting concurrency
cards/0/title: A channel is an async queue
cards/0/body:
Channel<T> is an asynchronous queue between parts of a program. A channel has two sides: Writer for producers and Reader for consumers. It's the async replacement for the "queue, lock and wait" combination: you wait on a channel with await, without blocking a thread.

Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>() accepts any number of items. Channel.CreateBounded<T>(100) holds at most 100. Here's what WriteAsync does on a bounded channel:

  • there's room: it adds the item and returns an already completed ValueTask, so the await goes through with no pause;
  • the channel already holds 100 items: it returns an unfinished ValueTask. The producer stops at the await, and the thread is free;
  • a consumer took an item: a slot frees up, the waiting writer's item goes into the channel, and its task completes.

This way a fast producer is forced to wait for a slow consumer. That's backpressure, like the generator's in the previous lesson. What happens when the channel is full is set in BoundedChannelOptions: the default is FullMode = Wait, and the DropOldest, DropNewest and DropWrite modes throw items away instead of waiting.
cards/1/q: A channel with room for 100 items is full. What does WriteAsync do?
cards/1/options/0: Returns an unfinished task: the producer waits asynchronously until a slot frees up
cards/1/explain: That's the default behavior, FullMode = Wait. The channel drops items only if you explicitly pick DropOldest, DropNewest or DropWrite.
cards/2/options/0: So a fast producer doesn't eat up memory when the consumer can't keep up
cards/2/options/2: You can't create a channel without a bound
cards/2/explain: On an unbounded channel WriteAsync never waits. If the consumer can't keep up, the queue grows until memory runs out.
cards/3/title: End of the stream and several consumers
cards/3/body:
ReadAllAsync() returns an IAsyncEnumerable<T>. await foreach over it waits for the next item while the channel is empty, and it ends only when the channel is completed and empty. The producer completes the channel: Writer.Complete() means "no more is coming". The readers drain what's left, and their await foreach exits. Forget Complete, and the consumers wait forever, so the pipeline's task never completes.

  • After Complete you can't write: WriteAsync throws ChannelClosedException.
  • Complete(ex) completes the channel with an error: after draining what's left, a reader gets an exception instead of a normal end of the loop.
  • There can be several consumers. Each item goes to exactly one of them: they share the stream of work rather than each getting a copy. It's a queue, not a broadcast.

Step by step for the code below. Four consumers start and stop at the await: the channel is empty. The producer writes while there's room, and each item taken frees a slot. After the last job the producer calls Complete — in a finally, so that the consumers exit even if it fails, and its own task carries the error. Each consumer that sees a completed, empty channel leaves its loop. WhenAll completes when all five are done.
cards/4/q: The producer has finished. What does the consumer print?
cards/4/options/0: 0…9, and "done" is never printed: the channel isn't completed, so await foreach waits for the next item
cards/4/options/1: 0…9 and "done": the producer finished, so there's no more data
cards/4/options/2: 0…9, then InvalidOperationException: there's nothing more to read
cards/4/explain: The channel doesn't know the producer is done: the producer's task finishing tells the channel nothing. To a reader, an empty channel that isn't completed means "wait". You need ch.Writer.Complete() after the loop, preferably in a finally.
cards/5/q: Two consumers read one channel through ReadAllAsync. The producer wrote 100 items and called Complete. How many does each get?
cards/5/options/0: 100 between them: each item goes to exactly one, and how they split depends on their speed
cards/5/options/1: 100 each: both get a copy of every item
cards/5/options/2: Exactly 50 each: the channel hands items out strictly in turn
cards/5/explain: A Channel is a queue: an item that's taken disappears from it. Whoever is free first takes the next one. If you need to send to everyone, give each recipient its own channel.
cards/6/body:
Since .NET 6 you can process a collection asynchronously with a concurrency limit. The mechanism: ForEachAsync starts up to N worker tasks. Each one takes the next item from a shared enumerator, calls the body, awaits it and takes the next item. So no more than N bodies run at once, and 10,000 requests won't go out all together.

  • N is set in ParallelOptions.MaxDegreeOfParallelism. If you don't set it, the default is Environment.ProcessorCount: there's always a limit.
  • The body gets a token ct. On the first exception ForEachAsync cancels that token, and the workers stop taking new items. When the bodies already started finish, the ForEachAsync task completes with an error, and await throws the body's exception.
  • Your own token goes into ParallelOptions.CancellationToken: ct in the body is canceled along with it.
cards/6/code:
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(urls,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8 },   // at most 8 bodies at once
    async (url, ct) => await DownloadAsync(url, ct));     // ct is canceled on the first error
cards/7/q: You need to download 10,000 files, at most 8 at a time. What do you pick?
cards/7/options/2: A sequential await in a loop
cards/7/explain: WhenAll limits nothing by itself: all 10,000 requests go out at once and swamp the server. A sequential loop downloads one at a time and takes about 8 times longer. ForEachAsync keeps exactly 8 downloads running.
cards/8/q: Parallel.ForEachAsync is called without ParallelOptions on a machine with 16 logical cores. How many bodies run at once?
cards/8/options/0: Up to 16: the default limit is Environment.ProcessorCount
cards/8/options/1: All of them: without MaxDegreeOfParallelism there's no limit
cards/8/options/2: One: without options the loop is sequential
cards/8/explain: ForEachAsync always has a limit. But for I/O the number of cores is an arbitrary figure: the API may handle more or fewer. So it's better to set the limit explicitly.
cards/9/explain: The limit is MaxDegreeOfParallelism. CancellationToken and TaskScheduler are ParallelOptions properties too, but you can't assign a number to them, and there's no Timeout property.
cards/10/title: The same by hand: SemaphoreSlim and WhenAll
cards/10/body:
You can build the same limit from the lock lesson: each download first takes a slot from a semaphore. new SemaphoreSlim(8) means 8 free slots and no upper limit. Step by step:

  • 1. Select calls the lambda for each url, and ToArray creates all 10,000 tasks right away.
  • 2. The first 8 get a slot: WaitAsync returned a completed task, and the download starts.
  • 3. The other 9,992 stop at await WaitAsync. They're just waiting tasks in the semaphore's queue; they hold no threads.
  • 4. A download finishes, and the Release in finally hands the slot to the next waiter.
  • 5. WhenAll completes when they're all done and returns an array of results in url order (section 2).

The difference from ForEachAsync: here all the tasks are created at once, 10,000 objects in memory, but WhenAll hands you an array of results. ForEachAsync keeps only N bodies running and takes items as it goes, and you collect the results yourself. A third way is a channel with N consumers, from the start of this lesson.
cards/11/q: The limit doesn't work: all 10,000 download at once. Which line is to blame?
cards/11/explain: WaitAsync without await is the same fire-and-forget from the first lesson. The ninth call gets an unfinished task, throws it away and goes straight to downloading. The compiler would have warned you: CS4014.
cards/12/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/12/options/0: Each item in a channel goes to exactly one consumer
cards/12/options/1: Without Writer.Complete(), await foreach over ReadAllAsync never ends
cards/12/options/2: Parallel.ForEachAsync has a limit even if MaxDegreeOfParallelism isn't set
cards/12/options/4: A Channel stores data on disk
cards/12/explain: WhenAll waits for whatever you give it; limiting is up to you: with a semaphore, ForEachAsync or a channel with N consumers. A Channel is an in-memory queue.
cards/13/pairs/1/1: A limit: the writer waits when there's no room
cards/13/pairs/2/1: "No more is coming": readers leave the loop
cards/13/pairs/3/1: Read until the channel is completed and empty
cards/13/pairs/4/1: N worker tasks over one collection
